content: Recommendations that are weak in nature should be clearly justified, and any changes made to them must be explicitly and transparently documented. It is essential to create an environment that facilitates the adoption of these recommendations, including promoting behavioral changes among healthcare practitioners to support evidence-based practices. Local professional societies can play a significant role in this process, and an inclusive and participatory approach should be encouraged. The WHO’s Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health (MCA) Department has extensive experience in integrating WHO guidelines and tools into national healthcare programs. Monitoring and evaluation mechanisms should be embedded within the implementation process to derive critical insights for improving uptake and ensuring sustained application. Strong recommendations will be prioritized when assessing their impact on the quality of care. Numerous studies have explored various aspects of postnatal care, including home-based versus hospital-based care, early discharge practices, and the role of community health workers in reducing neonatal mortality. For example, randomized trials have examined the effects of early postpartum discharge combined with nurse visitations, the impact of breastfeeding education on feeding patterns, and the efficacy of peer counseling in promoting exclusive breastfeeding. Research has also highlighted the importance of interventions such as chlorhexidine application to umbilical cords to prevent neonatal infections and mortality, as well as community-based strategies to improve perinatal and neonatal care. Studies from diverse settings, including rural India, Pakistan, and sub-Saharan Africa, have demonstrated the effectiveness of integrated maternal and newborn care packages in reducing neonatal mortality. Additionally, clinical algorithms and simple criteria have been validated to identify severe illnesses in neonates during routine household visits, enabling timely treatment or referral. Delayed initiation of breastfeeding has been shown to increase the risk of neonatal mortality, emphasizing the need for early breastfeeding promotion as a critical intervention. These findings underscore the importance of evidence-based, community-driven, and context-specific approaches to improving maternal and neonatal health outcomes globally.
